title: God Said, and There Was — Light, Division, Good
blocks: Brothers and sisters, today we are opening Genesis chapter 1 together. This is the first page of the whole Bible, and it is also the first lesson of this entire course of study. Let me flag one thing before we begin: Genesis 1 is not a scientific report, and it is not a position paper in a debate about the age of the earth. It is a declaration — a declaration of who made this world, why he made it, and who you are.

So we are not going to rush at the question of how many hours those six days were — we will face that question honestly later on — because I want you first to see something more urgent than that. The picture at the opening of this chapter looks exactly like the messiest days you and I have ever lived through.
Formless and empty, darkness on the face of the deep. And then God did something: he spoke.
1. Chaos Is Not the Last Word

Brothers and sisters, let me start with a very practical question. Have you ever had one of those days when you open your eyes and everything is already in pieces? Work with no thread to pull, relationships in a tangle, bills and messages and responsibilities piled up, and inside you it is simply dark — you cannot even say clearly what it is you want.

Genesis 1:2 is a picture of exactly that: "The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep." The Hebrew behind "formless and empty" is תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (*tohu vavohu*), a rhyming pair that sounds like two hollow echoes. And notice: the text does not say the earth was *bad*. It says it was *not yet arranged* — waste, void, without shape, without content, without use.

And over that chaos, who moved first? "God's Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters." That word "hovering" is מְרַחֶפֶת (*merachefet*), and Deuteronomy 32:11 uses the same word for an eagle fluttering over her young. That is not an eagle on patrol. That is an eagle with her wings spread out to cover.

Brothers and sisters, hold that picture. Over the messiest stretch of your life there is also a pair of wings spread out. God does not wait until you have tidied yourself up before he shows up. While you were still nothing but chaos, he was already hovering over you.
So the first thing Genesis 1 tells us is this: chaos is not the last word. God has never been frightened of the dark, because he can speak to the dark.
If God can turn chaos into order with a single word, why is my situation still a mess after all this praying?

Be careful with this verse: do not read "God said, and there was" as "God speaks and I see it immediately." In this very chapter God takes six days, not one second — and when light is made on day one, the sun, moon and stars do not appear until day four. Order is laid down layer by layer; it does not arrive all at once. The mess you are still in may be sitting at day two or day three, and you simply cannot see the whole picture from where you stand. The confidence this text offers is not "God will work on my timetable"; it is "chaos is not the last word." So when you have prayed a long time and still see nothing, the question to ask is not "Is God doing anything at all?" but "What is he separating in this stretch?" God's order of work is to divide first and then to fill. Very often what we are asking for is the filling, while what he is doing is the dividing.
2. God Said, and There Was — a World Spoken into Being

The rhythm of this chapter is so simple you will remember it after one hearing: "God said … and it was so." That phrase "God said" appears ten times in chapter 1. Ten times. The author is perfectly capable of varying his sentences; he wants you to hear that beat. This universe was not hauled into place. It was spoken into place.

Verse 3: "God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." In Hebrew, "let there be light" is two words: יְהִי אוֹר (*yehi or*). Between the command and the accomplishment there is not a single syllable of gap. No struggle, no strain, no shortage of materials. He spoke, and it was.

Brothers and sisters, notice one small thing. God did not first drive the darkness out; he brought the light in. The moment light entered, darkness withdrew on its own. This is how the whole Bible deals with darkness. You do not have to clear every mess out of your life before you are qualified to let God in — the order runs the other way. Light comes in, and then the darkness goes.

Then verse 4 says, "God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness." Here is the second key verb of the chapter: to divide, in Hebrew וַיַּבְדֵּל (*vayavdel*). And it is causative — light and darkness do not separate themselves. God separates them.

For the next three days God keeps doing the same thing: on day one he divides light from darkness, on day two the waters above from the waters below, on day three the sea from the dry land. Then over the last three days he fills each of those three spaces in turn: day four the lights, day five the fish and the birds, day six the animals and the man.

Do you see the structure? The first three days make space; the last three days fill it. That is not a casual arrangement, that is how God works: draw the boundary first, then put the contents in. Brothers and sisters, this matters enormously for us. A life with no boundaries does not become richer by having more crammed into it; it only becomes more chaotic. The order God gives you is: divide first, then fill.
"God said, and there was" — so if I declare something in faith, can I speak things into being too?

This is the most commonly hijacked verse in the chapter, and the distinction has to be clean. From beginning to end this chapter has exactly one subject: God. "God said" occurs ten times, and not once is it a human being speaking. When the man is made, the first work God gives him is to *tend* and to *keep*, not to *create*. Our words carry weight because we are made in his image — that is why Scripture says death and life are in the power of the tongue. That means our words can build a person up or tear a person down; it does not mean our words can call something out of nothing. To move "God said, and there was" onto your own lips is to put the creature in the Creator's chair, and that is precisely what this book spends chapter 3 onward taking apart. The healthy use runs the other way: because he speaks and it is, I can hand him, without anxiety, the thing I have no words for.
3. A Light from the Original: One Word for "Create", One Word for "Saw"
Let us stop and look at two Hebrew words. These two will show you where the weight of the chapter lies.

The first word is "create", בָּרָא (*bara*). Throughout the Old Testament this verb keeps one very particular rule: its subject is always God, without a single exception. A human being can *make* (עָשָׂה), a human being can *form* (יָצַר), but a human being cannot *create*. That word is reserved for God.

Brothers and sisters, there is a great comfort hidden in that small grammatical rule. You will do many things in this life and shape many things, but there is one thing you never have to carry: bringing something out of nothing. That is not your job. The thing you cannot carry today may well be heavy precisely because you have taken בָּרָא onto your own shoulders.
The second word is "saw", וַיַּרְא (*vayar*). In this chapter, "God saw that it was good" occurs seven times. God works, and looks, and pronounces it good.

And that word "good", טוֹב (*tov*), is not a moral verdict; it is closer to "fit for the purpose it was made for." A knife is good because it cuts. A tree is good because it bears fruit. So when God says "good" he means: that is right, that is what I wanted it to look like.

Now put the two verbs side by side: God creates, and God sees. And then in Genesis 3:6 the text says that the woman "saw that the tree was good for food" — the same verb *saw*, the same word *good*, only the subject has changed. From God looking and pronouncing good, to a human being looking and pronouncing good for herself. Brothers and sisters, humanity's first catastrophe began with the question of who has the right to say that something is good.
If God saw that it was good, does all the evil in the world today mean God misjudged?

The word behind "good" is טוֹב (*tov*), which means "fit for purpose, working as it should" — not "incapable of going wrong." What God called good is the world he made; the evil that enters from chapter 3 onward is traced by the text very plainly to human choice and to the serpent, not to a defect in the workmanship. And notice too that the "saw" of chapter 1 is רָאָה, a word carrying inspection and responsibility — a craftsman who inspects his own work is exactly the God who will not walk away from it in the end. So the evil in the world is not evidence that God misjudged; it is evidence that God has not yet finished. The last book of the Bible says, "Behold, I am making all things new," in precisely that tone: he has looked it over, and he will deal with it himself.
4. In Our Image — Who You Are

At verse 26 the tone of the chapter suddenly changes. Up to this point, in making everything else, God has simply said "let there be." But when it comes to making the man, he first stops to deliberate: "Let's make man in our image, after our likeness."

That "our" has been read several ways down the centuries: some read it as a foreshadowing of the Trinity, some as God addressing the heavenly council, some as a royal self-deliberation. We handle that question in detail in the map of disputed issues. What I want you to catch today is the tone: to make the stars took one sentence; before making you, God stopped to confer.

The word "image" is צֶלֶם (*tselem*). In the ancient Near East, when a king conquered a territory he would set up a statue of himself there, announcing: this land is under my rule. So "the image of God" is first of all not something you possess; it is a commission you have been given — you stand here representing that One.

That is why verse 28 follows immediately: "Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion." "Have dominion" (רָדָה) is royal vocabulary — it means to rule. But notice where it sits: right after "in the image of God." Which is to say: only rule that looks like God's rule counts. God's reign is blessing, provision and rest; that is the pattern you have been authorised to follow.

Brothers and sisters, this one verse settles three questions at once. First, your worth is not something you earned; it was given — which means nobody can take it away. Second, the image is identity, not performance; so the elderly man with dementia, the child in the womb, and the person who just offended you all carry that image. Third, whatever patch you have been given to manage — a field, a company, or a few children — is to be managed after the likeness of that One.
Is being made in God's image the same as saying human nature is basically good?

No. "Image" (צֶלֶם) speaks of identity and commission — representing him, resembling him, managing on his behalf. It answers "who am I and for whom do I live?" "Basically good" is a claim about moral substance. From chapter 3 onward the image is not cancelled, but it is distorted: Adam is still made in the image of God, and yet he hides, he shifts the blame, he is afraid of God. So Scripture says two things at once — human beings have immense dignity (Psalm 8) and profound corruption (Romans 3) — and the two do not contradict each other. Here is where it shows up in practice. If I believe human nature is basically good, my expectations of people will be disappointed over and over. If I believe people are made in God's image and yet have fallen, I can honour every single person and still never treat anyone as my saviour.
If human beings bear God's image, do the unborn, the elderly with dementia and those in a persistent vegetative state still count as fully human?

They do, and this verse is precisely where their case is made. The image of God does not hang on capacity — it is not conferred on those who can think, work or respond. The text says God created humanity *in his own image*: that identity is given in the making, not earned afterwards. So a child still in the womb, an elderly woman who can no longer say your name, a man lying in a bed unable to move — their worth is exactly equal to yours and mine, because that worth is not held in their hands. It is held in the hands of the One who made them. This is also why Genesis 9:6 says, "Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image." Scripture pins the weight of a human life directly onto this identity.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is reading this chapter as a scientific paper. Some use it to prove the age of the earth and others use it to disprove the age of the earth; both sides push hard, and both may be asking the wrong question. This chapter answers "who made it and why" — not "how many seconds did it take." The moment you fall out with a brother or sister over the length of the six days, you have already left the purpose of this chapter behind.

The second is turning "the image of God" into human capability. People say the image is reason, or creativity, or moral sense. Each of those brushes against something true, but the danger comes right behind: if the image equals capability, then a person whose capability declines has less of the image. Psalm 139 says God covered us in the womb; that unborn child who cannot yet think has not one fraction less of the image.

The third is preaching "subdue the earth" as a licence to exploit it however we please. This verse has genuinely been misused that way. But read it through — Genesis 2:15 says God put the man in the garden "to cultivate and keep it." That is a gardener's work, not a logger's. Someone who squeezes the land dry is not carrying out this verse too zealously; he has not understood it at all.

The fourth is preaching "very good" and never getting to the three chapters that follow. Some turn Genesis 1 into a lesson in positive thinking: you are good, you were made very good, you must affirm yourself. Half of that is true, but preaching only that half breeds an optimism the text will not support. After the "very good" of chapter 1 comes the hiding of chapter 3. Human dignity and human fallenness have to be preached together, or the gospel has nothing to stand on.

The fifth is turning the passage about the sun, moon and stars into an astronomy lesson. The real point of verses 14 to 16 is that the text refuses even to use the words "sun" and "moon", calling them only "the greater light" and "the lesser light." In an age when every surrounding nation was worshipping the sun and the moon, that is an audacious sentence: those things you bow down to are two lamps that were hung up there.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the elders in my family talk about Pangu splitting heaven and earth, about heaven and earth arising of themselves — does that clash with Genesis? My answer is: affirm first, then distinguish. Almost every ancient culture on earth preserves a memory that in the beginning there was a beginning, and that fact is worth noticing in itself — Romans 1:19 says that what may be known of God has been made plain, for God has shown it to them. So the reverence your elders carry for "Heaven" is not superstition; it is genuine religious instinct. The distinction lies here: Pangu is part of what was made, born out of the chaos; the One the Bible speaks of stands outside the chaos and before all things. You can say it to your elders like this: you are right, heaven and earth do have an origin — and I have since learned that the One who opened them has a name, and he speaks.

The second question: were those six days twenty-four hours or not? Brothers and sisters, let me tell you honestly that godly scholars who love the Lord and hold equally to the inerrancy of Scripture differ on this one. Some hold that they are consecutive twenty-four-hour days. Some point out that the same word "day" already covers the whole creation period in Genesis 2:4. Others hold that the six days are a literary framework, the first three making spaces and the last three filling them. The position of these notes is that we do not adjudicate the age of the earth, because that is not what the text is for. But let me draw your attention to one detail — each of the first six days says "there was evening and there was morning", and only the seventh does not. The author left that gap open. Hebrews 4 tells us why: because that day has not ended, and you may enter it today.
If I have to ask God about everything, won't I end up too afraid to decide anything?

What this verse guards against is not carefulness; it is using prayer as a way of stalling. The test is simple: real enquiry says, "If God says no, I will not do it," while stalling says, "I am not ready to carry the consequences." The normal pattern Scripture gives us is this — God has already made the great principles plain in his word, and for a great deal of what remains he wants us to judge with a mind he has renewed (Romans 12:2). So the healthy order is: act on what you already know, and keep a heart that can be stopped at any moment while you are acting. If a person is paralysed waiting for a voice before he can decide whether to change jobs or whether to apologise, that is usually not godliness; it is fear of responsibility. God gave us his image, and making decisions was part of the gift.
7. Living 321 Out — Listen to Him First, Then Speak
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the beat of this chapter is "God said", and John 1 tells us that the One who was speaking is the Word, and the Word became flesh. On earth the Lord Jesus also worked by his word: he healed with a word, he stilled the storm with a word, he called a dead man out with a word. So my example is very concrete: listen to him first, then speak. A person who always speaks first and rarely listens first does not look like the God of this chapter, and does not look like the Lord who became flesh.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter gives that word "standard" its roots. This world is not a random accident; it was spoken by a God who has speech and order. Precisely because of that, his word can be a stable standard for us. A person who believes the universe has no author will in the end find it hard to believe his own life has meaning.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the One hovering over the chaos in verse 2 is the Spirit of God. Notice when he appears: not after everything is in place, but while there is still nothing at all. So when you feel you have nothing and everything is in pieces, that is exactly the terrain the Holy Spirit is most used to working in.

Let Jesus be King — the "dominion" of verse 28 is an entrusted office, not ownership. Letting Jesus be King means putting a new label on the patch in my hands — work, family, time, money — and the label reads "his", and I am only the steward. It is an easy sentence to say, and it will change how you make every decision.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — this chapter has exactly one protagonist from beginning to end. The man does not appear until day six, and he is the last item made, not the most important one. Human dignity is real, but humanity is not the centre. Putting yourself back in the place of a creature is not self-abasement; it is returning to our originally intended position.

Establish God's system — God's system is divide, then fill, and finally rest. That gives us a very practical warning: building a system is not endlessly adding things, it is drawing boundaries first. If your home, your small group, your ministry has plenty of noise but no order, that is not flourishing. That is going back to chaos.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We often say "change the mindset and you change the life", and the direction of that sentence is right — but it must not be taken as automatic cause and effect. Romans 1:21 says that some people, "knowing God, didn't glorify him as God" — knowing and not changing is entirely possible. So the complete statement is this: a mindset lit up by the Holy Spirit, plus a will surrendered to God, plus practice and accountability inside a community — that is when a life actually changes.
"Listen to him first, then speak" — but I am flat out every day. Where am I supposed to find time to be still?

This verse is not asking you to find an extra stretch of time; it is asking you to trade one. The order in chapter 1 is "there was evening and there was morning" — a Hebrew day begins in the evening, which is to say it begins with sleep. In other words, God is at work while I am asleep, and when I wake I am joining a work he is already halfway through. For busy people that is an enormous release: you are not holding this day up by yourself, you are being brought into it. So the practical step is not to squeeze out forty minutes; it is to give God three minutes at the head of the day — hear one sentence from him before you open your phone. When time is short, the first thing we cut is usually the most important thing; those three minutes are exactly what you must protect.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "Let There Be Light"

Brothers and sisters, the same chapter of Scripture, falling into different hearts, grows completely different things. Let me set four kinds of heart side by side; perhaps you will find yourself among them.

There is the proud heart. He finishes chapter 1 chiefly interested in which side of the debate he is standing on, and he goes home with three arguments ready to demolish somebody. 1 Corinthians 8:1 says, "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Brothers and sisters, from the first verse of this chapter to the last, not one line is about how much you understand. It is saying one thing only: there is One who was there before you.

There is the fearful heart. He hears "six days", "evolution", "the age of the earth" and tightens up, afraid he has believed the wrong thing, afraid of being cornered by a question. To that heart I want to say: your salvation does not rest on whether you can answer that question. The steadiest sentence in the chapter is the first one — in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Hold that, and you can learn the rest slowly. You have all eternity for it.

There is the ashamed heart. He feels he has achieved nothing, that he is old and useless, that all this talk about the image of God has nothing to do with him. Brothers and sisters, the image is given, not earned. God made you in his own image before you had done anything at all; and on the day you can do nothing at all, that image will still be there. This is not motivational talk. This is what verse 27 says.

And there is the wounded heart. Somebody once shut him up with the line "God made you good" — how can you be depressed? How dare you say you are not well? Brothers and sisters, look carefully: chapter 1 says "very good", and chapter 3 records the fall. Scripture has never asked you to pretend you are intact. Psalm 147:3 says, "He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds." God does not need you to put on a good face first. Healing is what he came to do.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, say one sentence out loud every morning. Before you look at your phone, say to God: "Lord, this day is yours; please speak." Put "God said" ahead of your own words, and the order of the whole day changes.

Second, find the most chaotic patch in your life and write it on paper. Do not rush to solve it. Do one thing first, following the order of this chapter: divide. Hand back to other people the responsibilities in that patch that belong to them, and push what does not belong to this week into next week. God's first move on chaos is to divide, not to work overtime.

Third, do the "seven times seeing" exercise. This chapter says God saw seven times that it was good. This week, before each day ends, find one thing God did today that you can call good, and write one line. Seven days in a row, then read it back.

Fourth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: the first page of the Bible is not proving anything, it is announcing that the world has an author; his way of dealing with darkness is not to drive the darkness out first but to bring the light in; and before he made human beings he stopped to confer, which means your worth was not earned, it was given.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my chaos is not the last word, because God can speak to chaos.
I declare that I will no longer try to make something out of nothing by myself, because creating is God's office and not mine.
I declare that my worth is given and not earned, and therefore no one can take it away.
I declare that everything in my hands is entrusted, and I will manage it after the likeness of the One who entrusted it to me.
If I practise "listen first, then speak" this week and I simply cannot hear God speaking, what then?

Start by getting the definition of "hearing" right. In Scripture God's primary way of speaking is his word, not an impression in your chest — so the most solid form of "listening to him" is to read the sentence he has already finished saying. If you read Genesis 1:3 this morning, you have heard him. What has to be dealt with next is not "did I hear?" but "having heard, will I do it?" And do not treat your quiet time as a signal-strength test; that only makes a person more anxious the harder he tries. The practical method is: read one sentence, write one sentence answering "what does this ask me to change today?", then go and do it. Once you have done it you will find that God begins to speak inside your days — he often does not speak first in the silence; he speaks more clearly after obedience.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, let it be the five words of verse 3: "and there was light."
Picture it: total darkness, nothing there, nothing to push against, no material to work with. And then a voice, saying two words — and the light was there.

And 2 Corinthians 4:6 says, "seeing it is God who said, 'Light will shine out of darkness,' who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." Brothers and sisters, Paul takes Genesis 1 and moves it straight into your heart and mine. The same God, the same act. However he spoke to that chaos then, he speaks that way today to the darkest patch inside you.
So this chapter is not a distant piece of history. It is a guarantee: as long as he is still speaking, you still have hope.

The focus is not on how much I understand about the mechanics of creation, not on which side of the debate I am standing on, and not on how much of a mess I feel today. The focus is on Jesus — he is the One who speaks, and he is the Light. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week, that we would be still, and that the Spirit who hovered over the chaos would say inside us too: let there be light. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.

1. ★ Somebody says, "Genesis 1 clashes with science, so there is no point reading it too seriously." Having heard this lesson, how would you answer? Say it in your own words; do not recite the manuscript.

2. ★★ "Formless and empty" (תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ) and "God said, and there was" sit in the same chapter. Why does the text write the mess first and the word second? If the order were reversed, what would be lost?
3. ★★★ God's way of making the world is to divide first and then to fill. How does that order differ from the way you normally handle a mess?
4. ★★ "Let's make man in our image" — where does that sentence place a person's worth? How is it different from "I am useful, therefore I have worth"?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can sort this out myself), fearful (this mess is more than I can carry), ashamed (someone like me does not deserve to be called good), wounded (nobody has ever said one good word to me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a patch inside you that you have decided will never come right? When did you pass that sentence on it?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The old idea about God that this lesson dismantled for me is …" If the answer is "none", say so honestly — that itself is an important discovery.
9. ★★ This week, on which patch of chaos will you make your first act of dividing? Name the time, the place and the person; do not just say "I'll try harder."

Leader's reminder: questions five and seven will touch wounds. If someone weeps, stop the discussion and stay with him; do not rush to supply an answer, and never say to a weeping person, "you need to have more faith." If long-term hopelessness or depression is involved, follow up privately afterwards and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "Listen to him first, then speak" — in your home this week, who most needs to be heard out first? Say that person's name, and what you will do.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: what about your workplace or your school?
12. ★★★ The three-minute practice: this week, read one sentence of Scripture before you open your phone each morning. Say which slot you will put it in and how you will remind yourself.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and share your answer to question five with him this week. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, the Bible does not open on a beautiful scene; it opens on a mess. Second, the first thing God did was speak, and then he separated the mess out layer by layer. Third, so I believe that chaos is not the last word. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one act of dividing you will do this week, and who you will tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to say once more, over each of our own patches of mess, "Let there be light."
